editorial_policy.rule: Only sources with approved display rights may be bulk rendered. Reference-only and pending sources must never be copied into the corpus until provenance, edition, license and checksum are recorded.
editorial_policy.ai_rule: AI may explain and synthesize, but Scripture text, source metadata and citations remain deterministic and separately identified.
editorial_policy.copyright_rule: Modern copyrighted commentaries are represented only by bibliographic metadata unless a license or written permission explicitly permits full-text display.

commentary.literary: The opening clause functions as the programmatic beginning of the biblical creation account.
commentary.lexical: The Hebrew verb bārāʾ is used here with God as subject; the verse presents creation as God's sovereign act.
commentary.catholic: Catholic interpretation reads creation as the free act of the one God and as the beginning of salvation history; doctrinal synthesis should be checked against the Catechism and magisterial sources rather than inferred from one verse alone.
commentary.historical: The text belongs to the ancient Israelite scriptural tradition. Historical and literary questions should be distinguished from the theological affirmation that creation depends upon God.
commentary.archaeology: Archaeology can illuminate the Ancient Near Eastern setting and material cultures surrounding biblical Israel, but it cannot excavate the theological act of creation itself.

fathers.summary: A major patristic reflection on creation, time and the meaning of 'beginning'.

preacher.title: Creation begins in God
movements: God is prior to all created reality
Creation is gift rather than accident
Creation opens the history that culminates in redemption
Faith in the Creator grounds gratitude, stewardship and hope
preacher.caution: Do not turn the verse into a simplistic scientific claim; keep theological, literary and scientific questions properly distinguished.

commentary.literary: John deliberately opens with language that echoes Genesis and immediately places the Logos before creation.
commentary.lexical: Logos can carry senses such as word, reason or discourse, but in the Johannine Prologue it functions personally and is identified in relation to God and as God.
commentary.catholic: Catholic Christology reads this verse within the whole Prologue and the Church's confession of the eternal Son: distinct in relation and truly divine, not a creature.
commentary.historical: The Prologue uses Jewish scriptural and wisdom language while speaking in Greek terms intelligible in the wider first-century Mediterranean world.
commentary.archaeology: This verse is theological rather than topographical. Archaeology contributes to the historical world of the Gospel but does not by itself adjudicate the metaphysical claim about the Logos.

fathers.work: Homilies on the Gospel of John
fathers.summary: Emphasizes the pre-existence and divinity of the Word and warns against reducing the Son to a creature.

fathers.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
fathers.summary: Reflects on the eternal Word, divine unity and the mystery of the Son's relation to the Father.

catena.summary: Patristic chain designed for Gospel-by-Gospel study. Only editorial summaries and source pointers are enabled until the selected public-domain edition is provenance-locked.

preacher.title: The eternal Word enters our history
movements: The Word does not begin at Bethlehem; He is already 'in the beginning'
The Word is personally related to God
Christian discipleship begins by receiving the divine Word who later becomes flesh
preacher.caution: Do not isolate one Greek clause from the whole Prologue or present lexical observations as if they replace the Church's Trinitarian confession.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.historical_note: Central city of biblical Israel/Judah and the principal setting of the Passion, Resurrection and earliest Jerusalem Church.
places.archaeology_note: Excavations across the city illuminate multiple periods, including Iron Age and Second Temple Jerusalem. Individual identifications must be evaluated site by site.

places.name: Bethlehem
places.historical_note: Biblically associated with David and, in the Gospel tradition, the birth of Jesus.
places.archaeology_note: The traditional Nativity site is centered on the Church of the Nativity; historical claims should distinguish continuous Christian tradition from what archaeology alone can prove.

media.title: Church of the Nativity from Manger Square

places.name: Nazareth
places.historical_note: Galilean town associated with the Annunciation tradition and Jesus' upbringing.
places.archaeology_note: Rock-cut tombs and domestic remains contribute to the evidence for a Jewish settlement in the Roman period; devotional identifications of particular structures require separate evaluation.

places.name: Capernaum
places.historical_note: Galilean lakeside settlement prominent in the public ministry of Jesus.
places.archaeology_note: Excavated village remains, later synagogue structures and the house complex traditionally associated with Peter are important for reconstructing the settlement's history.

places.name: Corinth
places.historical_note: Major Roman-period city associated with Paul's mission and correspondence.
places.archaeology_note: The forum, bema and civic remains illuminate the urban setting in which Pauline Christianity developed.

places.name: Ephesus
places.historical_note: Major city of Roman Asia linked with Paul's ministry and an early Christian community.
places.archaeology_note: The theater, streets, public buildings and cultic remains provide a concrete urban context for Acts 19 and early Christianity in Asia Minor.

places.name: Rome
places.historical_note: Capital of the Roman Empire and major setting for the final chapters of Acts and the early Roman Church.
places.archaeology_note: Urban monuments, catacombs and early Christian sites illuminate the social and religious environment of Roman Christianity; apostolic-site traditions should be identified as traditions where appropriate.
